Marshall to sue patients (CNN, The Hill, Washington Examiner). Marshall and Hamilton debate tonight, with Decision Desk HQ giving Democrats a 56 percent chance at the Senate (The Hill). Republicans keep attacking Trump's Russia sanctions waiver as Rubio and Wright give different explanations (Axios, The Hill). Trump endorsed Netanyahu nine days before Israel's vote, Vance declined to, and Iran says no uranium leaves (Axios, CNN, Fox News). In France, the interior minister offered to resign and unions plan a Nov. 5 strike (Fox News, NBC). **A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion**, though Meta beat on revenue and says it will appeal (CNBC, Axios). Tesla beat estimates but slipped after hours, and the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all rose Tuesday (CNBC). On the engineering side, **NASA's nuclear-powered SR-1 aims to launch in December 2028** (NASA, MIT Technology Review). Science brought the **first known green star**, a white dwarf polluted by planet debris (Space.com).

stories.title: Trump uses the word 'Shylock' at a Kansas rally while defending Sen. Marshall's medical-debt lawsuits
stories.summary: CNN, The Hill and the Washington Examiner report the remark, and CNN's fact check finds no law required Marshall to sue patients.
story: President Trump used the term "Shylock" on Monday, Oct. 19, at a rally in Park City, Kansas, while defending Sen. Roger Marshall, according to CNN, The Hill and the Washington Examiner. He was responding to a New York Times investigation that found Marshall's medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called the remark "disgusting," and the Anti-Defamation League said the word can "reinforce harmful tropes about Jews," The Hill reports.

CNN's fact check, published Wednesday, tested Trump's claim that Marshall would have broken a law by not suing. It found no law that requires a doctor to sue patients and none that requires 18 percent interest. The White House cited two federal laws that require reasonable collection efforts, but CNN notes those laws allow providers to forgive debts for patients who cannot pay. Marshall's campaign did not say which law Trump meant. Marshall's attorney said Marshall was not personally involved in decisions to seek warrants or garnish wages.

The Washington Examiner headline says Trump used the term "again," a reference to a similar remark at an Iowa rally in 2025, when he said he had never heard it as an antisemitic term (CNN, The Hill). Kansas is now a toss-up. The Hill reports that a Hill/Emerson poll had Democrat Adam Hamilton ahead 45 percent to 43 percent, and Decision Desk HQ's polling average has him up 0.4 points.
Marshall and Hamilton hold their second and final debate tonight at 7 p.m. Central on Nexstar's WDAF. How Marshall handles the medical-debt question will be the main thing to watch.
facts: Trump spoke at a rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday, Oct. 19.
A New York Times investigation found Marshall's practice sued more than 700 patients.
CNN found no law requiring doctors to sue patients over unpaid bills.
Schumer called the remark "disgusting" (The Hill).
The ADL said use of the word can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews (The Hill).
The final Marshall-Hamilton debate is tonight at 7 p.m. Central.
stories.left: Democrats say the remark is antisemitic and that Trump repeated it after being warned last year. They add that the legal defense does not hold up, since CNN found no law forcing Marshall to sue. For them the story is about a senator who had patients arrested over small debts while voting on health policy.
stories.right: Marshall's side says judges, not doctors, issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, and that the practice wrote off many bills and gave away millions in charity care. Trump's defenders argue the attack on Marshall is a campaign hit built on a decades-old practice. Conservatives who dislike the word itself say the party cannot dismiss the criticism, because it distracts from a Senate seat the GOP needs.
stories.next: Watch tonight's debate and any Republican senators who speak up on the remark; Kansas votes Nov. 3.

stories.title: Trump starts his busiest campaign week as Democrats are slight favorites to take the Senate
stories.summary: Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 56 percent chance at the majority, and some GOP senators worry Trump hurts them with independents.
story: Trump is spending the final two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms campaigning mostly for Senate Republicans, according to The Hill and Fox News. Fox reports rallies in Kansas on Monday, North Carolina on Tuesday and South Carolina on Wednesday. The Hill says the planned stops also include Iowa, Florida, Georgia, Michigan and Texas.

The Senate is split 53-47 now. The Hill cites Decision Desk HQ, which gives Democrats a 56 percent chance of winning the majority and Republicans 44 percent. The Hill also reports that the RNC moved more than $44 million to the party's House and Senate committees between mid-August and mid-October.

Some Republican senators question whether Trump helps. The Hill reports that GOP senators warn he is hurting the party with independents. Sen. Thom Tillis, asked whether Trump might lash out after a bad night, said "I think there's a risk, I really do." CNN's midterm live coverage describes Trump raising alarm about Democrats as he tries to limit losses.
The tour is a bet that turnout from his base matters more than persuasion. Kansas, North Carolina and South Carolina are the states where that bet is most visible this week.
stories.flag: The DDHQ odds are one forecaster's model; other forecasters differ.
facts: The Senate is split 53-47 today.
DDHQ gives Democrats a 56 percent chance at the majority (The Hill).
Trump rallied in Kansas, North Carolina and South Carolina on Oct. 19-21 (Fox News).
The RNC says it moved more than $44 million to the NRCC and NRSC (The Hill).
Tillis said there is a real risk Trump lashes out after a bad night (The Hill).
stories.left: Democrats argue Trump's approval, near record lows in Reuters/Ipsos polling, makes him a drag in swing states. They see Kansas and South Carolina moving their way and say voters are reacting to prices, the Iran war and the Russia waiver. They want the final weeks to be a referendum on him.
stories.right: Republicans say Trump is the only Republican who can turn out low-propensity voters, and that polls have underrated him before. They argue the tour puts resources where the Senate will be decided and that Democratic candidates are running on a map that favors them only in a bad news cycle. Some conservatives say a poor night would still be a narrow loss in a midterm.
stories.next: Early voting continues and the Nov. 3 election is 13 days away; Kansas's debate tonight is the next marker.

stories.title: Trump's waiver of Russia sanctions draws fire from Republicans as his team gives mixed explanations
stories.summary: Rubio says the White House wants a 60-day review, Wright calls the diesel deal a carrot, and Rubio also says Russia would sell its diesel anyway.
story: The backlash over Trump's order waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Russia sanctions law is now about the White House's own explanations, according to Axios. Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the diesel deal a "carrot" that could ease Russia's assault, Axios reports. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russia would sell its diesel anyway, and that Trump wants a 60-day review of how the Graham Act affects the global and U.S. economies.

The Hill reports that Sen. Thom Tillis called the move "beyond irresponsible" and Sen. John Cornyn said the late Lindsey Graham "would be appalled." Graham's successor, Sen. Darline Graham, said she disagrees with the decision and would keep pressure on Russia. House Speaker Mike Johnson said he warned the White House of "unintended consequences," The Hill reports. A separate letter led by Tillis asks the administration to rescind a Treasury general license that lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the moves on NBC's Meet the Press, saying "no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump" and pointing to 2025 sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil. The Wall Street Journal editorial board, quoted by The Hill, wrote that Trump "stuck a shiv in the back" of Graham's legacy. CNN reports that Ukraine also objected.
The Graham Act lets a president waive penalties by certifying to Congress that it serves the national interest, so lawmakers have no quick way to reverse it.
stories.blindspot: Most coverage found is from center outlets and the right-leaning Wall Street Journal editorial board; no standalone left-leaning article was found.
facts: Trump issued the waiver Oct. 16 (CNN).
Rubio says the White House wants a 60-day review of the Graham Act's effects (Axios).
Wright called the diesel deal a "carrot" (Axios).
Tillis, Cornyn, Johnson and Sen. Darline Graham have criticized the move (The Hill).
Bessent says no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than Trump.
stories.left: Democrats say the waiver gives Putin money and leverage while Russia keeps attacking Ukraine's energy system. They stress that Republican senators who wrote the law are now objecting, and they want Congress to force a vote. The mixed explanations, in their view, show there is no plan.
stories.right: The administration argues cheaper energy helps American families before the midterms and that the pause is a bargaining chip toward a peace deal. Foreign-policy hawks, including the Wall Street Journal editorial board, say it undercuts a law named for a Republican hero and rewards Moscow without a concession. A smaller libertarian wing sees sanctions as a cause of higher prices.
stories.next: Watch for a Senate letter, hearing or vote on the waiver, and the end of the 60-day review in mid-December.

stories.title: California's largest state worker union holds its first statewide strike, with pickets in Oakland, San Francisco and Sacramento
stories.summary: About 95,000 SEIU Local 1000 members are eligible to walk out over pay, health costs and Newsom's return-to-office order.
story: SEIU Local 1000 began a one-day strike on Wednesday, Oct. 21, the first statewide walkout in the union's 44-year history, according to KQED. About 95,000 state workers are eligible to strike. CalMatters reports the union is holding demonstrations in more than a dozen cities, including Oakland, San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego and Sacramento, where members plan a march to lawmakers' offices near the Capitol.

The contract expired June 30. KQED says the union wants across-the-board raises of 20 percent over three years, more state money for health coverage and remote-work rules set by each department. In late September the Public Employment Relations Board found that CalHR "refused to meet and confer in good faith." On Oct. 16 the board let the strike proceed once the union exempted more workers, mostly at state prisons. Fewer than 5,000 employees at corrections, Caltrans and state hospitals must work.

The DMV, the Employment Development Department and State Parks could see delays, and CalMatters says the state's agencies have contingency plans. Newsom's order requiring most workers to be in the office four days a week took effect in July after a one-year delay. The union's president has said the union will escalate if the state keeps bargaining in bad faith, according to CalMatters.
A Washington Examiner editorial argues government unions have shown Newsom who is in charge on the work-week fight. It is opinion, not news reporting, and does not cover today's strike itself.
stories.blindspot: Right-leaning outlets have not covered the strike itself in the search results; only an older Washington Examiner editorial on the return-to-office fight turned up.
facts: The strike is Wednesday, Oct. 21, and is the union's first statewide walkout.
About 95,000 workers are eligible; fewer than 5,000 essential employees are exempt (KQED).
The union wants 20 percent raises over three years (KQED).
PERB found CalHR did not bargain in good faith in late September (KQED).
DMV, EDD and State Parks services could be affected.
stories.left: The union says the state is bargaining in bad faith, a finding PERB itself made, and that workers who run the DMV and unemployment offices deserve raises as health costs and rents climb. It frames the four-day office order as a pay cut in commuting costs, and says remote work helps with recruiting.
stories.right: Critics say state workers have job security and benefits most private workers lack, and that a strike hurts Californians who need DMV and unemployment services during a budget squeeze. The Washington Examiner editorial says unions have outmaneuvered Newsom on return to office. Supporters of the mandate say public servants should work where the public is served.
stories.next: Watch whether the state returns to the table this week or the union announces further walkouts; Newsom leaves office in January.

stories.title: California's billionaire tax holds a slim poll lead, but two rival measures could cancel it
stories.summary: A September PPIC poll had Prop. 40 at 52 percent to 46 percent, and Newsom backs Prop. 42, which would ban new wealth taxes.
story: California's one-time billionaire tax, Proposition 40, led 52 percent to 46 percent among likely voters in a PPIC poll taken Sept. 4-10, according to KQED. PPIC's survey director called the lead slim and said supporters have "a lot of work to do." An earlier UC Berkeley IGS poll in August had it at 48 percent to 41 percent, CalMatters reports, with 70 percent of Democrats in favor and about 80 percent of Republicans opposed.

The tax can pass and still fail. CalMatters explains that Propositions 41 and 42 are written to override it. If all three pass and either 41 or 42 gets more votes than Prop. 40, the state cannot enforce the tax. In PPIC's poll Prop. 41, which would put new taxes under the state spending limit, led 51 percent to 44 percent, and Prop. 42 led 54 percent to 43 percent. Prop. 42 would also ban any new taxes on personal property.

Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes the billionaire tax and has endorsed Prop. 42, according to CalMatters, while the California Democratic Party backs the tax. The measure is backed by unions, and the SF Chronicle reports it qualified for the Nov. 3 ballot.
The most recent public poll found is from September, so the race may have moved.
stories.blindspot: Coverage found comes from center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning outlet article on the measure turned up in these searches.
stories.flag: The newest public poll found is from early September.
facts: Prop. 40 led 52 percent to 46 percent in PPIC's Sept. 4-10 poll.
Prop. 41 led 51-44 and Prop. 42 led 54-43 in the same poll.
If 41 or 42 gets more votes than 40, the state cannot enforce the tax.
Newsom opposes the tax and endorsed Prop. 42; the state Democratic Party backs the tax.
Election day is Nov. 3.
stories.left: Supporters say a one-time tax on the very wealthy would pay for health care and schools that federal cuts are straining, and that billionaires have gained far more than ordinary Californians. They say the rival measures are a trick by opponents to cancel a vote the public might otherwise approve.
stories.right: Opponents say wealth taxes drive founders and capital out of California, which relies heavily on a few high earners for income tax revenue. They argue that taxing unrealized assets is hard to value and sets a precedent that will reach more people. Newsom's own opposition shows this is not a partisan view in the state.
stories.next: Watch for a new PPIC or Berkeley IGS poll before the Nov. 3 vote.

stories.title: Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu splits Republicans as Iran restates its red lines
stories.summary: Trump endorsed Netanyahu nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 vote, Vance declined to, and Iran says no enriched uranium will leave.
story: Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Oct. 18, nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 election, according to Axios, NPR and Fox News (CNN dates it Saturday; the others say Sunday). NPR calls it the first time a U.S. president has explicitly endorsed a candidate in an Israeli election. Trump said that if Israel chooses anyone other than Netanyahu, America "will have to do this work ourselves" on Iran, Fox News reports.

Vice President JD Vance declined to follow, saying "I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections," CNN and the Washington Examiner report. Axios reports most polls show Netanyahu's coalition at 50 to 54 seats, short of the 61 needed, while polls from the Netanyahu-friendly Channel 14 show 63. Rival Gadi Eisenkot said Israelis alone will decide.

Fox News reports that Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote that no enriched uranium will leave Iran, and that President Masoud Pezeshkian said sanctions must be lifted and threats ended before talks. Trump said on Oct. 8 the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms (Axios, CNN). A White House official called an Axios report on a joint U.S.-Israeli strike plan "false."
The Dispatch's David Drucker has written that parts of the American right, especially younger populists, have grown cooler toward Israel.
facts: Israel votes Tuesday, Oct. 27; the U.S. midterms are Nov. 3.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Oct. 18 (Axios, Fox, NPR).
Vance said he is not getting involved in Israeli elections.
Rezaei wrote that no enriched uranium will leave Iran (Fox News).
Trump has said the U.S. will not attack Iran before Nov. 3.
stories.left: Progressives say Trump is turning a U.S. ally's election into a campaign prop and tying American security to one politician. They note polls show Netanyahu may fall short and argue the endorsement raises the odds of a new war with Iran that Americans do not want.
stories.right: Supporters say Netanyahu has been America's key partner against Iran and that Trump is just stating what is at stake. Pro-Israel conservatives say Vance's neutrality is an error. The populist right, including some commentators, argues the U.S. should not pick sides abroad, and says the split shows a real debate in the party.
stories.next: Israel votes Oct. 27; watch whether talks with Iran move before the Nov. 3 midterms.

stories.title: France's interior minister offers to resign after rioting as unions plan a Nov. 5 strike
stories.summary: Macron refused the resignation and ordered a review, and Trump says such riots won't happen in the United States.
story: France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered to resign after saying "in certain large cities, we lost control" during Saturday's protests, according to Fox News. Macron rejected the offer and ordered a review of what the Élysée called failures in planning and intelligence. NBC reports France is moving to impose curfews after its worst violence in years.

The French Interior Ministry said more than half a million people took part in Saturday's day of protest and nearly 2,400 were arrested, while organizers claimed about 800,000 (Fox News). CNN describes the rioting as a symptom of a larger political crisis ahead of next spring's presidential election. The protests began with high school students demanding better classrooms and spread to living costs.

Macron blamed "troublemakers from far-left fringe groups" while acknowledging protesters' legitimate concerns, Fox News reports. The head of the CGT union called strikes for Nov. 5 after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, with other actions planned Oct. 31 and Nov. 14. Fox News also reports Marseille banned demonstrations.
On Wednesday Trump said the United States will not put up with riots like France's, according to Fox News.
facts: Nuñez offered to resign; Macron refused (Fox News).
The interior ministry counted more than 500,000 marchers and nearly 2,400 arrests.
Unions plan strikes on Nov. 5, with other actions Oct. 31 and Nov. 14.
The protests began with high school students over school conditions.
France votes for president next spring (CNN).
stories.left: The left reads the unrest as anger over living costs and crumbling schools that the government has ignored. It says heavy policing and blaming far-left groups avoids the underlying grievances, and that unions are channeling the anger into a lawful strike.
stories.right: The right says the violence shows a loss of public order and points to the interior minister's own admission that police lost control. Some conservatives, citing Fox News, argue immigration and weak enforcement are driving it, and that National Rally and center-right parties can gain from the security debate.
stories.next: Watch the Oct. 31 and Nov. 5 actions and the results of Macron's security review.

stories.title: Markets expect the Fed to hold next week, but a CNBC analysis says Warsh could surprise with a hike
stories.summary: September CPI was 3.7 percent and the economy added only 29,000 jobs, and the 10-year yield sits near 5.15 percent.
story: The Fed meets Oct. 27-28 and markets expect it to leave rates unchanged, according to CNBC. A CNBC analysis argues that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh could still surprise with a rate hike, based on the inflation data. Officials raised rates a quarter point last month to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent, The Hill reports.

September consumer prices rose 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August, The Hill reports. Axios says Fed Governor Christopher Waller worries the acceleration could push inflation expectations up. The economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, well below the 80,000-plus economists expected, CNBC reports, and CNBC says the weak report cut the odds of an October hike.

Fed minutes showed officials see one more hike this year and none in 2027 as a group (CNBC). The data feed shows the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.15 percent and WTI crude at $97.89, both reflecting the inflation pressure. The Washington Examiner has run an op-ed arguing the Fed cannot create diesel or refining capacity by raising rates.
Warsh has avoided forward guidance, The Hill reports, which leaves the decision open until Oct. 28.
facts: The Fed meets Oct. 27-28.
September CPI was 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August (The Hill).
September payrolls rose by 29,000 (CNBC).
The Fed funds range is 3.75 to 4 percent (The Hill).
The 10-year yield is 5.15 percent and WTI crude is $97.89 (market data).
stories.left: Progressives and many economists say hiking into a weak jobs market risks a recession when much of the inflation comes from energy and war-related supply shocks. They want the Fed to look through oil prices and say workers should not pay for a war-driven price spike.
stories.right: Conservatives who favor tight money say Warsh must prove the Fed will not tolerate inflation near 4 percent after years above target, and that waiting repeats 2021-22 mistakes. Others on the right argue that rates cannot fix supply shocks in diesel or refining, citing a Washington Examiner op-ed, and blame energy and tariff policy instead.
stories.next: The Fed decision comes Wednesday, Oct. 28; the next jobs report follows in early November.

stories.title: Tesla beats Q3 estimates, but shares slip after hours as SpaceX merger talk looms
stories.summary: Adjusted earnings were 48 cents a share on $28.05 billion in revenue, and CNBC says shares traded about 2 percent lower after the close.
story: Tesla reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 48 cents a share on $28.05 billion in revenue after the close Wednesday, beating LSEG estimates of 43 cents and $27.88 billion, according to CNBC. CNBC says shares gave back early gains and traded about 2 percent lower after hours. Tesla had closed the day up 3.41 percent in the market-data feed.

Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the quarter, above the 469,000 Visible Alpha expected, and deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours of energy storage, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's preview. The preview had expected earnings and revenue to edge lower despite the delivery beat.

The earnings arrive a day after Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a merger, CNBC reports. SpaceX shares jumped 7 percent after it said revenue grew 161 percent in the third quarter. Tesla shares rallied with them on Tuesday, per CNBC.
CNBC's live page was inconsistent on the after-hours move, so the 2 percent decline is approximate.
stories.flag: CNBC's live coverage gave mixed readings on the after-hours move; no GAAP net income figure was found.
facts: Adjusted EPS was 48 cents vs. 43 cents expected (CNBC/LSEG).
Revenue was $28.05 billion vs. $27.88 billion expected.
Q3 deliveries were 486,532 vs. 469,000 expected (S&P Global).
Storage deployments were 13.7 GWh.
Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a merger (CNBC).
stories.why: Tesla is on Keanu's watchlist and has moved with SpaceX news all week. Investors now weigh a solid quarter against a possible merger, whose terms and timing are unknown. A beat that still drops the stock shows how much of its value rests on expectations about the merger and autonomy rather than the quarter.
stories.next: Watch the after-hours trading and the earnings call for merger comments; Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28.

stories.title: Meta beats on revenue even as a New Mexico judge orders a $25 billion privacy penalty
stories.summary: Meta's Q3 revenue was $64.60 billion, shares rose about 3 percent after hours, and Meta says it will appeal the penalty.
story: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion on Wednesday in a Cambridge Analytica-related privacy case, CNBC, Axios and Fox Business report. A jury found in September that Meta misled users about their data. Judge Francis Mathew calculated a maximum of $219.5 billion, using the state's $5,000 penalty across 43,899,720 violations, and cut it to $25 billion. Meta had asked for $3.45 billion.

Mathew cited willful violations, the length of the conduct and senior leaders' involvement, and found Facebook did not conduct the thorough investigation it promised, according to CNBC. Interest accrues at 15 percent a year. Meta's chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said "We are confident we will prevail on appeal," and called the case a tax on speech. One commentator expects a serious fight on appeal and does not expect Meta to pay anything near $25 billion.

Meta also reported third-quarter revenue of $64.60 billion against the $63.37 billion LSEG consensus, and its fourth-quarter guidance midpoint beat estimates, CNBC reports. The company narrowed its full-year capital spending range to $135 billion to $145 billion. Shares rose more than 3 percent after hours. CNBC's live blog says Zuckerberg committed to stay in California for eight years as part of a new share class.
Alphabet fell 1.62 percent in the market-data feed, and Microsoft and Alphabet report Oct. 28.
stories.flag: CNBC's live blog did not give a clear earnings-per-share comparison, so none is stated here.
facts: The penalty is $25 billion, reduced from a $219.5 billion maximum (CNBC).
Meta had asked for a $3.45 billion penalty.
Meta says it will appeal.
Q3 revenue was $64.60 billion vs. $63.37 billion expected.
Full-year capex is guided to $135-145 billion.
stories.why: A $25 billion penalty would be large even for Meta, but courts often cut such awards on appeal, which is why shares rose on the quarter. The case also shows how state attorneys general use consumer-protection law against big platforms. For investors in AI spenders, the narrowed capex range suggests spending is under better control than feared, one analyst said.
stories.next: Watch Meta's appeal filing in New Mexico and the stock open Thursday.

stories.title: Delhi cut electricity losses from about 50 percent to 5 percent, IEEE Spectrum reports
stories.summary: Private distributors, smart metering and anti-theft work took losses from more than half of power to 5 to 6 percent.
story: IEEE Spectrum reports that Delhi's power distribution losses fell from more than 50 percent in 2002 to 5 to 6 percent in 2026, and that grid reliability now tops 99.9 percent. The losses came from obsolete equipment and theft, which left utilities without money for upgrades.

The turnaround began in 2002, when the Delhi Vidyut Board was broken up and two private companies, BSES and North Delhi Power Limited, took over distribution. Tata Power-DDL, which took over North Delhi Power, inherited a combined commercial and technical loss of 53.5 percent, Spectrum says.

Spectrum's October issue frames the Delhi case as something other cities could copy. The magazine's earlier coverage of electricity theft describes the fix as a mix of better metering, network upgrades and enforcement. Some areas still have high losses, partly from illegal charging of e-rickshaws.
The lesson for engineers is that measurement comes first: you cannot fix losses you do not meter.
stories.flag: Both reports are IEEE Spectrum; the 5 to 6 percent figure is the more precise one.
facts: Distribution losses fell from more than 50 percent to 5-6 percent over about 25 years.
Reliability exceeds 99.9 percent (IEEE Spectrum).
Delhi's utility was split up and privatized in 2002.
Tata Power-DDL inherited a 53.5 percent combined loss.
Illegal e-rickshaw charging still causes losses in some areas.
stories.why: Grid losses waste generation that has already been built and paid for. The Delhi case shows that metering and governance can matter as much as new power plants, which is relevant as U.S. utilities face data-center demand growth.
stories.next: Watch for other cities adopting the Delhi model.

stories.title: NASA's SR-1 Freedom aims to be the first nuclear reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft by December 2028
stories.summary: NASA says the 48-kilowatt craft will carry three Mars helicopters, while MIT Technology Review says experts call the schedule ambitious.
story: NASA's Space Reactor-1 Freedom is planned as the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, NASA says. Its mission page lists a 20-kilowatt electric closed Brayton cycle power conversion system, HALEU fuel and a power and propulsion element producing 48 kilowatts, with a mass of about 12,000 kilograms.

NASA targets a late-2028 launch. Space.com reports December 2028, with arrival at Mars about a year later. It will carry SkyFall, three Mars helicopters evolved from Ingenuity. The power and propulsion element comes from the canceled Gateway station.

MIT Technology Review, which featured nuclear spaceships in its Oct. 21 "Impossible" issue, quotes NASA saying Idaho National Laboratory, which is building the reactor, is on target. The magazine says experts call the schedule ambitious and that little detail is public.
NASA frames SR-1 as a pathfinder to qualify the supply chain and build a workforce for later work, including the Lunar Reactor-1 surface power system.
stories.flag: NASA says the mission architecture is not final.
facts: Launch is targeted for late 2028 (NASA); Space.com says December 2028.
The reactor is being built at Idaho National Laboratory.
The spacecraft has a 20 kW electric Brayton power conversion system.
It will carry three SkyFall helicopters.
Experts call the schedule ambitious (MIT Technology Review).
stories.why: Nuclear electric propulsion could cut Mars transit propellant and power far larger instruments than solar arrays allow. A demonstration flight lowers the risk for surface reactors on the Moon and Mars, but the schedule leaves little room for a test failure.
stories.next: Watch for reactor ground-test milestones through 2027.

stories.title: Astronomers find the first truly green star, a white dwarf polluted by rocky planet debris
stories.summary: Space.com reports Mark Hollands's team found WD J1330+6435 about 326 light-years away, with sodium absorbing orange light.
story: A team led by Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick reports the first known genuinely green star, according to Space.com. The star, WD J1330+6435, is a cool white dwarf about 326 light-years away. Space.com published the report on Oct. 15.

The team's model says the star pulled in rocky material from a planetary companion. That material added calcium, lithium and sodium to its atmosphere. Sodium absorbs orange light, which shifts the star away from white or pale blue.

The team also found what could be the reddest star ever, white dwarf WD J1011+2845, and suggests white dwarfs could glow in many colors, including green, pink, cyan, yellow and purple, Space.com says. Hollands has published earlier work (2020) linking alkali metals in white dwarf atmospheres to ancient planetary crusts in Nature Astronomy.
The result rests on one press-covered report; the paper itself and outside experts were not found.
stories.flag: Only Space.com's coverage and an earlier Hollands paper were found; the new paper and independent expert reaction were not.
facts: The star is WD J1330+6435, about 326 light-years away.
Sodium in its atmosphere absorbs orange light.
The material likely came from a rocky planetary companion.
A second white dwarf may be the reddest star known.
Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick led the team (Space.com).
stories.why: White dwarfs that swallow planet debris let astronomers read the composition of rocky worlds from starlight. The color finding gives another way to spot such systems, though it needs confirmation from the underlying paper.
stories.next: Watch for the peer-reviewed paper and independent follow-up spectra.

stories.title: Ancient proteins identify more Denisovan remains in southwest China
stories.summary: Nature papers on Bianfu Cave used protein analysis to confirm hominin bones and teeth as Denisovan, including the first Denisovan arm bone.
story: Nature published 2026 papers on Denisovan remains from Bianfu Cave in southwestern China. One paper used ancient proteins to identify the hominin bones and two teeth as Denisovan, a group known mainly from a few fragments and DNA. A second paper covers how these Denisovans lived and what they ate.

Science reports that a partial elbow from the site is the first Denisovan arm bone identified, and that the fossil and primitive tools suggest the Denisovans were strong and agile hunters. Nature has also run a news piece saying archaeologists identified skulls from China as Denisovan, though that article could not be opened.

Earlier work covered the Harbin "Dragon Man" skull, which Nature and Science reported as likely Denisovan, based on proteins and DNA recovered from tooth plaque. Protein analysis helps because DNA rarely survives in warm regions.
The new papers widen the known range and body form of a group that interbred with modern humans.
stories.flag: The Nature news item on Denisovan skulls could not be opened, so its details are not reported here.
facts: The papers describe remains from Bianfu Cave in southwestern China.
Ancient proteins confirmed the bones and two teeth as Denisovan.
A partial elbow is the first Denisovan arm bone identified (Science).
Proteins survive where DNA often does not.
Nature also published a paper on Denisovan subsistence strategies.
stories.why: Denisovans have been defined mostly by genes, so fossils with bodies and tools show how they hunted, moved and spread. Protein methods let researchers identify remains from warm regions where DNA fails.
stories.next: Watch for further skull and bone identifications from sites in China.

stories.title: Nvidia and Recursive release open models built to run on a laptop or PC
stories.summary: Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and Recursive's Flint target local use, and the performance claims come from the companies.
story: Recursive released Flint on Oct. 21, a free coding model that runs on a laptop, according to TechCrunch. It is a mixture-of-experts model that uses 2.5 billion of its 40 billion parameters for any task. On Nvidia's RTX Spark it topped 150 tokens per second. It is free to download on Hugging Face.

Recursive says its automated research system, the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step, so a small team built Flint in under four months. CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce's former chief scientist, leads the company, which emerged from stealth in May with $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation. TechCrunch calls Flint an early public test of recursive self-improvement, and notes it is an AI research assistant overseen by people.

On Oct. 19 Nvidia released open-weight models for agents. TechCrunch reports Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, 120 billion parameters, targets enterprise agents, and Bolt 74B-A9B runs locally on RTX Spark PCs and DGX Spark workstations. A smaller Bolt E4B arrives later this month. Nvidia's claim that Super VL outperforms some models from Anthropic and OpenAI is unverified.
Both launches point to agents that run on local hardware, keeping code and data private.
stories.flag: Performance and build-process claims are the companies' own, and TechCrunch is the only outlet found.
facts: Flint is a mixture-of-experts model with 2.5B active of 40B parameters.
It topped 150 tokens per second on Nvidia's RTX Spark.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has 120 billion parameters.
Bolt 74B-A9B is available now; Bolt E4B is due later this month.
Nvidia's claims about outperforming other labs' models are unverified.
stories.why: Models that run on laptops reduce usage fees and keep source code on the device. If the benchmarks hold up, local agents become a real alternative to cloud APIs for coding and enterprise work.
stories.next: Watch for independent benchmarks of Flint and Bolt, and Bolt E4B later in October.

stories.title: OpenAI buys Orchestra Bio to expand its drug-development AI
stories.summary: Axios and TechCrunch report that OpenAI will fold the startup's agents into its Rosalind life-sciences model.
story: OpenAI acquired Orchestra Bio, a four-year-old startup, on Oct. 20, according to Axios, which had the exclusive, and TechCrunch. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Orchestra builds AI agents for operational work in drug development, such as tracking finances and resolving clinical-trial scheduling problems. Axios says scientists can hand off tasks like monitoring studies and spotting timeline delays. TechCrunch reports Orchestra had raised about $20 million as of 2025 from Andreessen Horowitz, Atria and 8VC.

OpenAI plans to fold the team and technology into Rosalind, its life-sciences model, and Rosalind Workbench, which helps researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI already counts Moderna and Novo Nordisk as Rosalind customers.
TechCrunch notes that OpenAI and Anthropic are both moving into science and pharma.
facts: The acquisition was announced Oct. 20.
Terms were not disclosed.
Orchestra had raised about $20 million (TechCrunch).
OpenAI will fold it into Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench.
Moderna and Novo Nordisk are Rosalind customers.
stories.why: Drug development spends heavily on coordination work, not only chemistry, so agents that handle trial logistics could shorten timelines. The deal also shows frontier labs buying specialist teams to enter regulated industries.
stories.next: Watch for Rosalind customer announcements and similar deals from Anthropic.

briefs: Nvidia says its Nemotron 3.5 Super VL matches larger models on instruction following, and the claim is Nvidia's own (TechCrunch).
IEEE Spectrum reports Energy Dome's CO2 battery, a 20 MW, 200 MWh plant in Sardinia, is being adopted for grid storage, with Google backing deployments (IEEE Spectrum).
Nature News reports a large study suggesting body-clock disruption contributes to one in four cases of depression; the study details were not available (Nature).
Phantom Neuro reported successful procedures for an under-skin EMG implant that controls prosthetic arms in an early human trial (IEEE Spectrum).
Cook's Kansas rating and polling put the Senate race at a toss-up, with a Hill/Emerson poll showing Hamilton up 45 percent to 43 percent (The Hill).
